q: A grower in a marginal northern region carts in dark crushed rock and spreads it between the rows. What is he trying to buy?
opts: A warmer soil surface, since dark material absorbs more of the light landing on it
Protection from fungal disease, since the dust settles on the leaves and dries them
A supply of nitrogen, released from the rock as the winter frosts shatter it
A higher soil pH, since crushed rock releases lime as it slowly breaks down
exp: A dark surface takes in what a pale one throws back, and two or three degrees at soil level is worth having where the season barely finishes. The gain is concentrated at the ground, though: it warms the soil the roots start in and the air just above it, and fades away long before the top of the canopy.

q: Under a covering of large stones the soil stays damp well into a hot dry summer, while the bare earth alongside has baked out. What are the stones doing?
opts: Feeding the soil beneath them with minerals as they dissolve away over the course of a season
Shading the vine's leaves from the worst of the afternoon sun and the heat that comes with it
Drawing water up from the water table by capillary action through the gaps between them
Acting as a mulch, cutting the evaporation of water from the surface
exp: A stone layer breaks the contact between wet soil and dry air, so water that would have evaporated stays where a root can still reach it. That is one of the reasons a stony vineyard floor is valued in hot dry country, and why growers there think twice before clearing the stones off.

q: Two blocks at the same latitude, one on dark stony ground and one on cold heavy clay, and the stony block buds a week earlier every year. What does that early start also bring?
opts: A harvest date noticeably later than the neighbouring block
A markedly higher incidence of powdery mildew in the canopy
A greater exposure to damage from a late spring frost
A reduced risk of frost damage, since the buds harden as soon as they open
exp: Warm ground brings the whole cycle forward, which is a gift at the end of the season and a hazard at the beginning of it. The block that buds first is the one holding tender green shoots when a late frost arrives, so the property that ripens the fruit reliably can also cost the crop outright.

q: White pebbles are spread beneath low-trained vines in a cool region. Beyond warmth, what does the vine gain?
opts: Light bounced up onto the shaded underside of the canopy and the fruit
A measurable drop in the acidity of the ripening grapes
Some protection for the fruit against a summer hailstorm
Calcium, which the leaves take up directly from the dust
exp: Bunches hang in the shade of their own leaves, and light arriving from below helps to colour and ripen the skins. It is the practical argument for a pale vineyard floor, and it explains why a white soil is not simply the opposite of a dark one but useful in a different way.

q: Quartz sand, flint and weathered granite are gathered under one adjective, describing ground built on silica and inclined to be acid. Which word?
exp: Siliceous and calcareous are the two families a soil description usually starts from, and they behave in opposite ways: silica-rich ground is acid, holds little and warms fast, while lime-rich ground is alkaline and keeps a reserve. Most vineyard soils are some mixture of the two.

q: Deep beds of pale silt stand in a vertical face when they are cut, and were laid down grain by grain over thousands of years. Which agent delivered them?
exp: Wind-laid deposits are called aeolian, after the Greek god of the winds, and the one every wine student meets is loess. Because wind sorts by weight, the particles are all much of a size, which is why such beds are so even and why they drain far better than their fineness suggests.

q: Rock and earth creeping and washing down a hillside pile up at the foot of it in an unsorted heap. What is that material called?
exp: Colluvium is moved by gravity and gets no further than the bottom of the slope, so it stays mixed: boulders, gravel and fine earth all together. A deposit that has travelled further tends to arrive sorted by size instead, and the difference between the two shows plainly in the wall of a soil pit.

q: A soil analysis opens by naming the rock the soil weathered out of. What is that rock called?
exp: Parent material sets the chemistry a soil starts with, so ground off granite is acid and ground off limestone alkaline before anything else has happened to it. It is only a starting point: rainfall, age and farming can carry a soil a long way from what the rock beneath would suggest.

q: Some vineyard soils have rotted in place out of the rock directly beneath them, and others were carried in from somewhere else entirely. What is the first kind called?
exp: A residual soil sits on its own parent rock, so what is underfoot matches what is beneath. A carried soil may have nothing to do with the rock below it, which is why a geological map is a poor guide to a vineyard on its own and why the pit gets dug anyway.

q: A soil report describes a block as stony, or as skeletal. What is being said about it?
opts: It lies directly on bedrock with no subsoil between the two
A large share of its volume is stone rather than fine earth
Its organic matter has been exhausted by continuous cropping
It has never been ploughed since the day the vines went in
exp: Stones take up room without holding water or nutrients, so a skeletal soil behaves as though it were far shallower than it measures. That is generally the point: it drives the roots down and keeps the vine hungry, which is why stone content is recorded rather than dismissed.

q: Two ocean currents pass the southern tip of Africa, one cold and running north up the Atlantic seaboard, one warm and running south down the Indian Ocean side. Which of them does the cooling for the winelands?
opts: The Canary current, which runs down the north-west African coast
The Mozambique Channel drift, which runs down the far east coast
The Agulhas, which brings warm Indian Ocean water down the east coast
The Benguela, which carries cold water north along the west coast
exp: Water off the west coast is far colder than the latitude suggests, and the sea air and morning fog that come off it drop temperatures wherever a vineyard sits within reach. The Agulhas is real and it is warm, which is why the country's cool sites face the Atlantic rather than the Indian Ocean.

q: Rain arrives in the Cape winelands mostly between May and August, and hardly falls at all while the fruit is ripening. Which climate type does that pattern name?
exp: Winter-dominant rainfall with a hot dry summer is the Mediterranean signature, and it makes water rather than sunshine the limiting factor. Inland districts irrigate as a matter of course, while dry farming survives only where the soil can hold the winter rain deep enough to last.

q: A hard wind blows out of the south-east for days at a time through the Cape summer, dries the canopy and knocks back rot. What do locals call it?
exp: The nickname is a compliment: by scouring humidity out of the vineyard it holds back botrytis and powdery mildew, and it drops temperatures at the same time. The bill is paid at flowering, when a strong blow shakes off crop and thickens skins on what remains. A berg wind is the opposite thing, hot and dry off the interior.

q: A buyer plans a trip taking in every major Cape wine district, and never has to cross a provincial boundary to do it. Which province is he driving around in?
exp: The Northern Cape does grow vines along the Orange River, and there are token plantings elsewhere, but the Western Cape holds the overwhelming bulk of the industry. Everything outside it is either too hot, too dry or, on the eastern side of the country, too wet in summer.

q: Long ridges of folded rock run through the winelands and divide them into separate valleys, giving growers altitude and aspect that a plain could not. What are those ranges called?
exp: The Cape Fold Belt was thrown up about two hundred and fifty million years ago, when the southern edge of Gondwana was crumpled against the ocean plate grinding under it, and the Simonsberg, Helderberg, Hottentots Holland and Groot Drakenstein all belong to it. The ranges matter more than latitude here: they block or funnel the sea air, and they carry the vineyards that need height to stay cool.

q: Vines were planted at a Dutch supply post below Table Mountain within a few years of its founding, and the first Cape wine was pressed in 1659. What had the post been established to do?
opts: House a mission school for the interior
Victual ships on the sea route to the East Indies
Serve as a penal colony for the Dutch Republic
Work the alluvial gold of the Cape Flats
exp: Jan van Riebeeck's refreshment station stood halfway between Europe and the East Indies, and it existed to put fresh food and drink aboard passing fleets. Wine was thought to help against scurvy on the long haul east. That is why viticulture reached the Cape early and by a commercial rather than a monastic route.
